name: Maya Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the Westgate pension centre, on new state pension claims. Mostly I'm checking people's work records and sorting out gaps, like years they were caring for children or living abroad. The callers are mostly in their sixties, and some of them are very sharp and some are very confused. Linda, my team leader, checks my trickier cases, because I still get the overseas rules muddled.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day feel like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Calm, mostly. Headset on at nine, work through calls and post, lunch at the same table with the same three women. We're allowed a call-summary tool now, and I use it on the long calls, though I still type my own notes on the short ones. After work I usually help at my husband Kerem's family bakery for an hour, closing up the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Things get a bit easier, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a helpful tool, like a calculator, and leave it there. I'm not one to make big pronouncements. At the bakery I'd joke that the robots still can't knead dough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be happy. It's a steady job, the bakery's steady, and we have a few months put by. I'd be thinking about having a baby in a couple of years, not about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the summary tool for long calls and get the overseas rules sorted. I'd keep putting a hundred and fifty a month aside for when the baby comes. And I'd carry on helping at the bakery in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. This is the version where life goes the way I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the baby mean for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to go part-time for a while, which the pension centre allows. Kerem's mother would help, she's already asking. That's how it works in our family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing that could spoil this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bakery had a bad year. My husband's family bakery is our real safety net, so a bad winter for bread worries me more than any computer.

say: I'd call AI a **helpful tool**, like a calculator.
I'd joke at the bakery that robots **can't knead dough**.
think: My job and the **bakery** are both steady, with savings put by.
I'd be thinking about **having a baby**, not computers.
do: Use the **summary tool** on long calls.
Save **a hundred and fifty** a month for a baby.
Keep helping at the **bakery** in the evenings.
feel: **Calm** and content, as **life goes** to plan.
S0.quote: My husband's family bakery is our real safety net, so a bad winter for bread worries me more than any computer.
fieldNote: Her household's **family bakery** gives her a sense of security.
She uses AI **occasionally** and calmly, as a tool.
**Family plans**, especially a baby, are her main focus.

steps.text: Use the call-summary tool on long pension calls
Save a hundred and fifty a month for a baby
Keep closing up the bakery shop in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more worrying. Checking records is exactly what a computer would be good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to make sure older people can still speak to a person. Plenty of our callers can't use a website. I'd say it at work, gently, and to my mother-in-law, who'd agree loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the checking side goes to the computer and fewer of us are needed. The ones who stay would be the ones good with the tools and the difficult calls. I'm in the middle, so I don't know which side I'd land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools properly once the others had tried them, so I'm on the right side. I'd save harder, two hundred and fifty a month. And Kerem and I would probably wait an extra year for the baby, until I knew my job was safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be watching every team meeting for signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would waiting for the baby matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to be able to go part-time and come back to something. I don't want to come back from having a baby to find my desk at the pension centre has been turned into software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the bakery be a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could be, but it doesn't pay much. Kerem's father runs it like it's 1985. It feeds us, it doesn't make us comfortable.

fieldNote: She defends **older callers** who need a human voice.

steps.text: Learn the new pension-checking tools after colleagues try them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast. Our office has only just stopped using fax machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to look after each other, because no government can plan for that in two years. I'd say it at the mosque, and to my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's gone by 2028. Everything I do is on a screen and a headset. The bakery is hands-on, so it would last longer, until robots around 2031, and maybe people still want a family baker after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the bakery properly, learn to bake, not just close the shop, and help Kerem's father modernise it. We'd put off the baby until things were clearer. And we'd lean on the family, maybe move in with Kerem's parents above the shop to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Scared, but not alone. That's the difference family makes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you modernise the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Online orders, a delivery app, maybe a stall at the Saturday market. Kerem's father would hate it at first. My father-in-law still writes orders on the back of flour bags, and in two years that bakery would be our whole income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put off a baby. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad. We'd pray about it. But I wouldn't bring a baby into a house where nobody knew what next year looked like.

say: I'd say **families and communities** must look after each other.
I'd say it at the **mosque** and to my family.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**, since it's all screen and headset work.
The **bakery** lasts until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Join the bakery and **learn to bake** properly.
**Put off** having a baby until things are clearer.
Move in **above the shop** with my husband's parents.
feel: **Alarmed** and scared, but **not alone**, thanks to family.
S2.quote: My father-in-law still writes orders on the back of flour bags, and in two years that bakery would be our whole income.
fieldNote: She turns to **family and faith** before government.
She uses the **robot gap** by moving into the bakery.
Delaying a **baby** is a painful choice for her.

steps.text: Join the family bakery full time and learn to bake

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. You could plan with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the time sensibly: help small family businesses get ready, not just big companies. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd keep the pension job for three or four years and get the bakery ready in the evenings. By 2031 I'd be out of the office, and the bakery would have to be strong enough to carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Westgate and learn the AI tools there. In the evenings I'd set up the bakery's online orders and the market stall. And we'd put some of our savings into a new oven, because the old one breaks every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a steady kind. I like having a plan with dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't the bakery risky to put savings into?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but it's family. Putting our savings into a new oven feels safer than leaving the money in a bank while my office job disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in three years, once the bakery is on its feet. Kerem's mother is already counting.

The **bakery** must be strong enough to carry us by 2031.

fieldNote: She builds the **family business** while keeping her office income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to have a family and build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to prepare, for families or for government. Teach young people trades and help small businesses. I'd say it calmly, it's what I've always thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right. I'd keep the job for most of it, have our first child, and grow the bakery slowly. By 2036 the office goes, but the bakery's hands-on and lasts to about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and go part-time after the baby. We'd modernise the bakery bit by bit. And we'd put money aside every month for the business, not just for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled. Ten years feels like enough time to do things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the right order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marriage, baby, then business. We've done the first. With ten years of warning, I can have my first baby before I have to choose between a desk and the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Kerem's father won't let us change anything. He's stubborn. But ten years is long enough even for him.

I'd back **trades for young people** and help for small businesses.

do: Save monthly for the **business**, not just ourselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough to do anything in the right order. What would help is support for small family businesses to modernise, and keeping a human on the phone for older people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the older callers. A seventy-year-old woman ringing about her pension needs a patient voice, and I'm not sure a machine has patience or just speed.

headlineQuote: A seventy-year-old woman ringing about her pension needs a patient voice, and I'm not sure a machine has patience or just speed.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old** junior state pension caseworker at a regional pension centre.
She is **traditional** and practising, married to Kerem, whose family runs a bakery.
She uses AI **now and then** and is **calm** in AI Plateau.
She is **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, when she'd move into the bakery and delay a baby.
She leans on **family and faith**, and plans everything in the right order.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time to do things in the right order.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping a **human on the phone** for older callers.
